Chapter 6: The Limits of Sovereign Power and the Rights of Resistance
So, once we’ve laid out what absolute sovereignty means, there’s a natural question that comes up—are there any real boundaries to that power? Can those at the center ever be resisted, or are their commands always final?
Let’s take a closer look at where the lines are drawn, and how the social contract itself actually sets those limits.
Even though the sovereign’s power seems vast, it isn’t without checks. Its very legitimacy depends on one thing: protecting the lives and security of everyone it governs. That’s the core promise—if the sovereign fails to keep people safe, lets chaos take over, or even becomes a source of harm, then its right to rule starts to crumble. In other words, this social contract is a two-way street. People give up some freedoms, but only because they expect safety in return. The sovereign’s authority is only as strong as its ability to keep that bargain.
There are a few big ideas to keep in mind when we talk about these limits:
First, self-preservation. No one has to follow orders that put their life at risk. That basic instinct to survive is at the heart of the whole agreement, and it’s something you simply can’t give up.
Second, impossibility. You can’t be forced to do something that’s literally impossible. Laws and commands have to stay within what humans can actually do.
And third, basic justice. Sure, the sovereign has a lot of leeway, but if there’s ongoing cruelty or the government abandons public safety, it chips away at its own legitimacy.
Picture a town where the ruler, instead of being a shield, turns into a source of fear. The streets aren’t safe anymore, and the very person meant to protect everyone is now the biggest threat.
In moments like that, people’s duty to obey doesn’t just fade—it flips. Resisting isn’t just allowed; it’s actually a return to that core idea of self-preservation.
But here’s something to pay attention to—the bar for justified resistance is really high. Everyday frustrations, personal slights, or minor grievances don’t cut it. The danger of falling back into chaos is so great that only the most serious failures—where safety and order are truly lost—make resistance justifiable.
You can think of this as a scale. On one side, there’s the sovereign’s job to protect and keep order. On the other, there’s the people’s responsibility to obey, as long as their basic safety is looked after.
When that balance tips too far and protection disappears, the contract itself breaks down—and that’s when society starts looking for a new way to come together and rebuild trust.
